arc: The teaching names the five "drawers-upward" — the Five Sons of the Awakener — as the discrete ascending operations by which the spiritually dead are raised through the degrees back to the Father, gathered inward at the last into the image where they rest, and known in the cosmos by the various names of the sabbath-state.
reading:
This chapter announces, under the heading "Concerning the Five Sons of the Awakener," the structure of resurrection itself: "Of those who died — the resurrection is at hand." The whole teaching is the unfolding of how that resurrection happens. It does not happen in a single act but through five discrete drawings-upward, five operations of the Lord answering to the five faculties of the soul. Five here is the complete natural-rational structure: every degree at which a soul has been bound must have its own corresponding lift, or the soul is not wholly raised.

The five are listed in order of ascent. The first is the foremost, the lowest reach of the awakening into the deadened natural — the place where the Call must first take hold. The second is the second drawer-upward, lifting from the next interior. The third is named the First Father, which here functions as the inmost paternal pole into which the rising soul is being conducted — the source toward whom every motion of ascent is finally tending. The fourth is explicitly the Mind of Light, the illumined rational understanding: regeneration cannot complete itself without the awakening of spiritual intelligence, and so this fourth operation is the rousing of the inner mind into clear seeing. The fifth, "the last in his speech," is the consummating awakener: through his word "all the lives are gathered inward, and they go to him, and they rest in their image." This is the centripetal close of the whole process — every dispersed life-power is drawn home and finds rest in the likeness which is its true icon.

Read together, the five form a single ladder. Each "drawer-upward" is a station of vertical operation (the verb is consistently "raise" / draw upward, never "release"); together they constitute the column by which the captive Living Soul rises through the discrete degrees from the deadened natural up to the Greatness. The fifth's gathering-inward and the resting-in-the-image is the same movement that elsewhere is figured by the Pillar of Glory and the Last Andrias: the homeward column receiving its full freight, the redeemed soul finally conformed to its own true likeness.

The teaching then opens out into a list of the names by which the cosmos calls these awakeners — "Resolution," "Stillness," "the Fast," "the Day," "the Rest," "Peace." These are not separate beings but the qualities of the sabbath-state through which the resurrection is felt by those undergoing it. To be drawn upward is experienced as stillness after agitation, as fasting from the desires of the cosmos, as peace after war, as day after night, as rest after the long laboring of the natural under self-love. The Coptic preserves the connection: the body must be hushed from "all the desires of the cosmos" before the upward drawing can do its work, and so the awakeners are rightly named after that hushing.

The closing fragments anchor the ascent in its standing structures. The Pillar of Glory is named — the column of accumulated truth on which all the raised lives travel home. The ship of the living waters is named — the doctrinal vessel that bears truth and soul through the natural. One of the awakeners is "in glory," "in the Great Aeon," "established" forever; another is associated with the air in the cosmos, the medium of perception by which the Call descends and the Hearing returns. The teaching ends with the assurance that "these who raise up in the [Pillar/Aeon] forever" — "the Great One endures forever, unto the ages of ages." The resurrection is not a momentary rescue but a permanent operation: the five drawers-upward stand eternally as the architecture by which every dead soul that hears the Call is conducted, degree by degree, into the rest of its true image in the Great Aeon.

The lacunae are heavy in the central portion, especially around the names of the first, second, and fifth awakeners. The arc, however, is intact: announcement of resurrection, enumeration of five ascending operations culminating in gathered rest in the image, identification of these operations under the cosmic names of the sabbath-state, and grounding of the whole in the Pillar of Glory and the Great Aeon that endures forever.
